newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan closer to elections after Okinawa poll.
newsitem.headline: Japan closer to elections after Okinawa poll.

text.p: A modest turnout in Japan's first referendum on the thorny issue of U.S. bases on Okinawa puts Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto one step closer to an early general election, political analysts said on Sunday.
The referendum showed more than 90 percent of those voting in favour of a reduction of the U.S. forces but turnout was just 59.5 percent.

Activists had hoped for a turnout of 70 percent to give Okinawa governor Masahide Ota, the man leading the opposition to the U.S. presence on the island, a strong bargaining position in urging Tokyo to deal with the issue of the bases.
But Sunday's lukewarm turnout shows the problems of Okinawa will not be a major hindrance for Hashimoto who was reported to be preparing for an early general election, analysts said.

"Although it is still too early to make any predictions based just on the poll results, I think the election schedule will go as planned by party officials," said Tadashi Iyasu, politics professor at Ryukyu University in Okinawa.
Hashimoto struggled on Friday to quell growing media speculation that he planned to dissolve parliament and call a snap general election in October or early November.

Japanese newspapers cited unidentified senior officials in the ruling coalition as saying Hashimoto, believed to have been planning to wait until after January to dissolve parliament, had changed his mind under growing pressure from within his Liberal Democratic Party, which is ready for early polls.
"I have no plans to dissolve the Lower House for the time being because I must deal with such pending issues as Okinawa and economic recovery," Hashimoto said on Friday.
Hashimoto does not have to call elections until mid-1997, when the four-year term of the current Lower House expires.

The prime minister said he would decide the timing of the election after he meets Ota on Tuesday, while the governor is expected to clarify his stance on whether he will renew the land lease contracts for U.S. bases.
Ota began blocking the forced appropriation of private land for U.S. bases by refusing to renew land lease contracts after a rape of an Okinawan school girl by three U.S. servicemen last year.
Last month, Japan's Supreme Court ordered Ota to renew the contracts for the U.S. bases.
The contracts with 3,000 landowners, many opposed to the U.S. bases, expire next May. That could create a potential threat to U.S. use of the facilities and complicate U.S.-Japan security ties.
The success of Tuesday's talks, however, will depend on whether Hashimoto can convince Ota that Tokyo is strongly committed to resolving the bases issue.

Many Okinawans say that a U.S.-Japan agreement in April to reduce the amount of land occupied by U.S. bases by one-fifth does not go far enough to quell sentiment on the island, host to 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan.

The central government has pledged to trim Okinawa's bases and move unwanted activities like artillery drills to other parts of Japan, but regions named as alternate sites have rejected Tokyo's request.
Japanese and U.S. officials will hold high-level talks in Washington on the military bases and security ties later this month.
Hashimoto is due to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton at the end of September, when he will fly to New York to attend the annual opening session of the U.N. General Assembly.
